docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Communicating with chambers
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Communicating with chambers: He wants case-related questions handled through the docket, not by phone or email to chambers, and doesn’t accept informal letters from anyone. The Clerk returns them unread.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) report and discovery period
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) report and discovery period: He treats the report as critical and values one that outlines the main issues and flags likely discovery disputes. He decides for himself whether to hold a scheduling conference, considering your request. He generally defers to reasonable deadlines you propose and uses them in the initial scheduling order, but expects discovery to close six to nine months after the report is filed. He may enter a nine-month cutoff even if you ask for more unless you explain why. He modifies a schedule only for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Courtesy copies
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Courtesy copies: Unless ordered otherwise, within three business days after e-filing, deliver two paper copies of any filing over 20 pages, with all exhibits and attachments, to the Clerk’s office to his attention. Print double-sided when possible, from the docket with the ECF header, ordered and tabbed, and use a three-ring binder if they can’t be stapled. Don’t send brief routine procedural motions unless asked.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Motions: He doesn’t require a pre-filing conference for dispositive motions. Extension and adjournment requests under Local Rule 7(b) must state the original date, the number of earlier requests, whether they were granted or denied, and whether the other side consents. If it doesn’t, give its stated reasons. A motion to withdraw as counsel must show the client had actual notice, or it will be denied. He decides case by case whether to hear argument, may rule from the bench, and says briefing quality affects how fast he can rule. He welcomes junior lawyers arguing and may hear supplemental argument from senior counsel.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Discovery and settlement
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Discovery and settlement: He prefers to refer discovery disputes to a magistrate judge. He refers settlement conferences to a magistrate judge. If the parties agree one would help, file a joint request asking for the referral, and prepare well for it.

docs.t: Judge Omar A. Williams (D. Conn.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Omar A. Williams, D. Conn.. Trial: His trial preferences are in his Joint Trial Memorandum Instructions and his standing order on jury selection, which we did not read. Read both before you prepare a pretrial filing.

docs.t: Judge Miranda Du (D. Nev.) — Communications and copies
docs.x: Judge Miranda Du, D. Nev.. Communications and copies: She keeps a paperless chambers: don’t send courtesy copies unless she asks. File searchable PDFs under LR IC 2-2 and LR IA 10-1. Counsel are strongly discouraged from contacting chambers directly about case matters except as LR IA 7-1(a) allows. Use the standing order, or ask the courtroom deputy or Clerk’s office. Filings that don’t follow the Local Rules or her order may be stricken.

docs.t: Judge Miranda Du (D. Nev.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Miranda Du, D. Nev.. Motions: She decides jurisdictional motions, such as remand or lack of personal or subject-matter jurisdiction, before other motions, to avoid needless discovery. Otherwise motions are decided in the order filed unless one needs expedited treatment. Submit a proposed order, attached as an exhibit, with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including a motion for default judgment. When she grants a stay, any pending motions are automatically denied without prejudice, and a party may move to reinstate them when the stay lifts. File one consolidated motion in limine rather than separate motions on single issues.

docs.t: Judge Miranda Du (D. Nev.) — Trial and settlement
docs.x: Judge Miranda Du, D. Nev.. Trial and settlement: Trial is set after the settlement conference, or after the joint pretrial order if the case doesn’t settle, on the first available trial stack. Her standard Order Regarding Trial is filed once a trial is scheduled. A case usually goes to the assigned magistrate judge for a settlement conference after dispositive motions are decided, or as soon as the joint pretrial order is filed if there are none. Electronic devices are allowed for calendars and for presenting evidence or argument, but not devices that cause feedback or interfere with the court recording equipment. She strongly encourages lead counsel to let newer lawyers argue, examine witnesses and play a real role.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Courtesy copies and proposed orders
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Courtesy copies and proposed orders: Don’t deliver paper courtesy copies unless chambers asks. If asked, bind them and tab the exhibits. Submit a proposed order with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including default judgment. It can be an exhibit or a separate filing, and must also be emailed in Word format to his chambers address.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Hearings and junior lawyers
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Hearings and junior lawyers: Motions may be decided with or without a hearing under LR 78-1. Add a note in the filing, or a separate notice, that a lawyer with six or fewer years of experience will argue. If he is inclined to rule on the papers, that representation weighs in favor of holding argument. He will entertain a reasonable request for a senior lawyer to supplement the junior lawyer’s argument. He generally grants requests to appear by phone or video for just cause.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Staff, transcripts and technology
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Staff, transcripts and technology: Court staff may contact counsel about scheduling or trial status, and he strongly urges a prompt response. For expedited or daily transcripts, contact the court reporter as early as possible, because advance deposits likely will be required and a late request may be refused. Phones, iPads, laptops and printers are allowed to check calendars and present evidence or argument, but must be off until the judge permits. Use the courtroom’s presentation resources. Training is arranged through his courtroom administrator.

docs.t: Judge Andrew P. Gordon (D. Nev.) — Settlement, trial dates and jury instructions
docs.x: Judge Andrew P. Gordon, D. Nev.. Settlement, trial dates and jury instructions: Civil cases usually go to the assigned magistrate judge for a settlement conference after the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask in writing for an early settlement or pretrial conference under LR 16-2. Trial is scheduled after the joint pretrial order on the first available trial stack. His Order Regarding Trial is filed shortly before trial, and a sample is on his page. He has stock jury instructions drawn from the Ninth Circuit’s model instructions, posted on his page. Your proposed instructions need not repeat them unless you disagree with one. They must be concise, understandable and neutral, and argumentative instructions will not be given.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Courtesy copies, calls and PDFs
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Courtesy copies, calls and PDFs: Paperless chambers: no courtesy copies unless requested. For docketing, scheduling and calendar matters, call the courtroom administrator. Calls to chambers are only for urgent matters. File searchable PDFs under LR IC 2-2 and LR IA 10-1. He appreciates OCR on exhibits too, though the rules don’t require it.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Motions: Non-dispositive motions may be referred to the magistrate judge. Jurisdictional motions, such as remand or lack of personal or subject-matter jurisdiction, are decided before other motions. Submit a proposed order with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including default judgment. He will consider a stipulation or motion for a continuance or extension filed at least three days before the deadline. Later requests are granted only in extraordinary circumstances with just cause. When a stay is granted, pending motions are automatically denied without prejudice, and a party may move to reinstate them. Hearings aren’t scheduled automatically. Put “(Hearing Requested)” on the front page directly under the title of the motion, response or reply.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Appearances, transcripts and technology
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Appearances, transcripts and technology: He will consider a request to appear by phone or video for just cause. Notify the court reporter immediately on receiving his order if you need expedited or daily transcripts. Cell phones must be off while court is in session, and recording court proceedings is strictly prohibited. Phones, iPads, laptops and printers are allowed for calendars and presenting evidence, but not devices that cause feedback or interfere with recording equipment.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Settlement and trial dates
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Settlement and trial dates: A case is usually referred to the magistrate judge for a settlement conference under LR 16-5 after dispositive motions are fully briefed. He will usually stay the ruling until the conference has happened. With no dispositive motions, referral comes as soon as the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask in writing for an early pretrial conference under LR 16-2. Trial is scheduled after the settlement conference, or at the close of discovery. He rules on dispositive motions before the trial date. His Order Regarding Trial is filed as soon as trial is scheduled.

docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Joint pretrial order and trial procedures
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Joint pretrial order and trial procedures: Unless ordered otherwise, file a proposed joint pretrial order within 30 days after discovery closes. It must include the caption, trial counsel, jurisdiction statements, claims and defenses to be tried, trial days needed and jury or non-jury, whether all parties consented to a magistrate judge (without saying who did not), stipulations, witness list with summaries, deposition designations and objections, and an exhibit list. Mark one star for exhibits no one challenges on authenticity and two stars for exhibits no one objects to on any ground. Also file motions in limine, a pretrial memorandum if useful, requests to charge and proposed voir dire in jury cases, and proposed findings and conclusions in non-jury cases. docs.t: Judge Richard F. Boulware (D. Nev.) — Default judgment procedure
docs.x: Judge Richard F. Boulware, D. Nev.. Default judgment procedure: Prepare an order to show cause with the date and time of the conference left blank. File it with an attorney’s affidavit covering the basis for default, service, procedural history, whether default can be entered against fewer than all defendants, proposed damages and their basis, and why an inquest would be needed. Include a proposed default judgment, copies of all pleadings, the affidavit of service, and a Clerk’s certificate that no answer was filed if that is the basis. After he signs the order, serve the defendant with a conforming copy and the papers and file an affidavit of service before the signed order is filed.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Communications, copies and PDFs
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Communications, copies and PDFs: Counsel and parties are strongly discouraged from contacting chambers directly about case matters except as LR IA 7-1(a) allows. Call the Clerk’s Office or her courtroom administrator. She keeps a paperless chambers: no courtesy copies unless requested. File searchable PDFs under LR IC 2-2(a)(1). She appreciates OCR on exhibits too. Cell phones must be off in court, and recording is prohibited under General Order 2022-06.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Motions
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Motions: Non-dispositive motions generally go to the magistrate judge. Jurisdictional motions are generally decided first. Submit a proposed order with every stipulation and unopposed motion, including default judgment. She will generally deny a stipulation or motion for extension or continuance that lacks justification. When a stay is granted, pending motions are automatically denied without prejudice, and additional briefing on reinstatement needs leave of court.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Motions to seal and pro hac vice
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Motions to seal and pro hac vice: A motion to seal must comply with LR IA 10-5 and also state whether the compelling-reasons or good-cause standard applies and explain, with specificity, why the public’s right of access is outweighed, citing Center for Auto Safety v. Chrysler and Kamakana. Failure to explain may mean denial. A pro hac vice petition must follow LR IA 11-1. Attach certificates of good standing issued within six months before filing from every state or territory where the lawyer is admitted. Signatures are needed from the petitioning attorney, local counsel and the party. A non-compliant petition may be denied and the petitioner required to repay the filing fee.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Hearings and remote appearances
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Hearings and remote appearances: Hearings aren’t scheduled automatically. Put “(Hearing Requested)” on the front page under the title of the motion, response or reply. Motions are generally resolved without a hearing if no just cause is shown. Adding “Junior Attorney” under “Hearing Requested” makes a hearing more likely. File requests for phone or video appearances on the docket, no later than two business days before the hearing.

docs.t: Judge Gloria Navarro (D. Nev.) — Settlement, trial dates and transcripts
docs.x: Judge Gloria Navarro, D. Nev.. Settlement, trial dates and transcripts: A case usually goes to the magistrate judge for a settlement conference under LR 16-5, and she usually stays the ruling on dispositive motions until it happens. With no dispositive motions, referral comes once the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask for an early pretrial conference under LR 16-2, and an alternate magistrate judge will preside. Trial is set after the settlement conference using the dates in your Joint Status Report or Joint Pretrial Order, and she rules on dispositive motions first. Her Order Regarding Trial is filed as soon as trial is scheduled. For expedited or daily transcripts, submit the AO 435 form by email to the court’s transcript address. Advance deposits are likely and a late request may be refused.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Filing
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Filing: File everything on CM/ECF. Pro se parties are exempt, but counsel in a case with a pro se party must still e-file. Proposed orders for stipulations, unopposed motions and default judgments, and jury instructions, are filed on ECF, and chambers may ask for a Word copy by email. No courtesy copies unless requested. Unsearchable PDFs may be rejected. LR IC 2-2 and IA 10-3 require an index of exhibits, a descriptive cover sheet on each exhibit (not just “Exhibit A”), and each exhibit as a separate file. Violations can lead to denial of the motion without prejudice.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Emergency motions and sealing
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Emergency motions and sealing: Emergency motions should be rare under LR 7-4(b) and need a declaration signed by counsel. A motion to seal must follow Center for Auto Safety v. Chrysler and state the legal standard and the reasons, the legitimate interest, the injury if sealing is denied and why a less restrictive option fails. It needs sworn evidence where necessary and a narrowly tailored proposed order that lists each document or portion to be sealed in a table. Explore alternatives, minimize sealing, and redact instead of sealing whole documents. Non-compliance means denial.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Communications with chambers
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Communications with chambers: All communications must be in writing and filed on ECF, with copies delivered to any parties who don’t get ECF notice. Don’t send her copies of correspondence between counsel. Call the courtroom deputy for docketing, scheduling or calendar questions. Ex parte calls about the substance of a case are prohibited. If a submission needs immediate attention, phone chambers after filing on ECF. Respond promptly if chambers staff contact you.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Argument, appearances and stays
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Argument, appearances and stays: Motions may be decided with or without a hearing under LR 78-1. Note in the filing, or in a separate notice, that a lawyer with six or fewer years of experience will argue. That representation weighs in favor of argument when she is inclined to rule on the papers, and a senior lawyer may supplement. She generally grants requests to appear by phone or video for just cause. A granted stay automatically denies pending motions without prejudice, and a party may move to reinstate them.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Motions in limine
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Motions in limine: File a single consolidated motion in limine, after meeting and conferring under LR 16-3(a). Each side is limited to 10 motions in limine of 10 pages each, even with several plaintiffs or defendants, who must coordinate. Replies are discouraged.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Settlement, trial and transcripts
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Settlement, trial and transcripts: Civil cases generally go to the magistrate judge for a settlement conference after the joint pretrial order is filed. You may ask for an early settlement or pretrial conference under LR 16-2. Trial is set after the joint pretrial order on the first available trial stack. She encourages consent to trial by a magistrate judge under LR IB 2-2. Her Order Regarding Trial is filed shortly before trial. Devices that cause feedback or interfere with recording equipment aren’t allowed in court. Contact the court reporter early for expedited or daily transcripts, because advance deposits will likely be required.

docs.t: Judge Cristina D. Silva (D. Nev.) — Pro se litigants and habeas
docs.x: Judge Cristina D. Silva, D. Nev.. Pro se litigants and habeas: Pro se litigants must communicate with the court only in writing and keep their contact information current, or risk dismissal or default under LR IA 3-1. Counsel dealing with a pro se party must follow the Nevada Rules of Professional Conduct on unrepresented persons. In habeas cases with pro se petitioners, the respondent must serve the petitioner with the answer and the record when filing them, and the record must include a table of contents or index.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Hearings, copies and filing
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Hearings, copies and filing: He decides motions with or without a hearing under LR 78-1. If he orders one, his courtroom deputy will contact you, and if you don’t respond within 48 hours the court will set a time convenient to itself. Hearings and conferences are audio recorded and court reporters are usually not provided. Don’t submit paper courtesy copies unless requested. File searchable PDFs, and file each exhibit as a separate file, not part of the base document. Motions to seal must follow LR IA 10-5. A motion for leave to amend must follow LR 15-1 and also attach a redlined or highlighted comparison to the prior operative pleading.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Case management: After an answer, he generally orders an initial Joint Case Management Report, which you must draft by meeting and conferring and must follow strictly. He may set a case management conference that lead counsel must attend. For any later conference, each party files its own report at least 5 court days before it, no longer than 10 double-spaced pages. It covers discovery completed, discovery served but not answered, and unresolved discovery issues with the meet-and-confer efforts and the resolution each side wants. Attach nothing except the relevant discovery excerpts, privilege logs or deposition testimony.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Motions to dismiss and discovery
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Motions to dismiss and discovery: A motion to dismiss does not stay discovery. To stay discovery, file a motion that addresses the factors in Kor Media Group v. Green. A stay isn’t granted merely because a motion to dismiss is pending.

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Informal discovery dispute procedure
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Informal discovery dispute procedure: No discovery motion may be filed until you follow this procedure and he orders briefing. Lead counsel must first meet and confer in person, by video or by telephone. Letters, emails or a brief call don’t count. If that fails, the party seeking or resisting the discovery files a “Motion Regarding Discovery Dispute” of no more than 5 pages in 12-point type with one-inch margins. The only exhibits allowed are a declaration detailing the meet-and-confer (what was discussed on each request, concessions, and what was resolved) and a single exhibit reproducing only the disputed requests and responses. It must have separate sections for the unresolved issues, the party’s position with support, and the compromise it proposes. The opposing party files a response within 2 court days, also 5 pages, on the same terms. He then decid

docs.t: Judge Craig S. Denney (D. Nev.) — Emergency discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Craig S. Denney, D. Nev.. Emergency discovery disputes: During a deposition, after trying in good faith to resolve it, you may seek help under LR 37-1(b) by contacting his courtroom deputy or chambers. Before you do, email a short description of the dispute to his chambers address. If he is unavailable, the deposition continues with objections noted for the record.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Contacting chambers
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Contacting chambers: No letters in place of opposed extension requests, contested discovery, or substantive motions. Don’t copy her on letters to opposing counsel, and don’t send faxes or email. She permits no ex parte contact. Don’t call chambers with questions the rules answer. Case questions go to the courtroom deputy. Counsel may not communicate directly with her law clerks, and a clerk who contacts you does so at her direction. Read each order itself, because the docket description is sometimes inaccurate.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Argument and conferences
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Argument and conferences: She sets no regular days for argument or evidentiary hearings and schedules them ad hoc. She hears argument if it will help, and a party may ask in writing. She may hold telephone conferences on scheduling and motions and usually asks counsel to place the call. Bring matters to her only after discussing them with opposing counsel.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Motions, replies, and orders
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Motions, replies, and orders: Motion practice follows LR 7.3. She strongly urges following LR 7.6 on evidentiary objections. Absent leave and good cause, no reply or sur-reply may exceed ten pages. File a proposed order with every motion and response except dispositive motions, in Word or WordPerfect to her ECF mailbox. Title it “Order,” with no lawyer’s name, address, or client number. She is extremely reluctant to grant continuances, especially when counsel haven’t been diligent, but will consider good cause.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Working copies: Unless directed otherwise, deliver bound, tabbed copies to the Clerk’s Office within three days of filing injunctive-relief papers and any dispositive motion, brief, response, or reply that has an appendix or tabs. Courtesy copies of other motions are discouraged.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Summary judgment: Every summary judgment motion and opposition must recite the facts with complete, accurate record citations. She won’t consider any fact not supported by a citation. Give pinpoint cites such as the document title, a deponent’s name and pages, or an affidavit’s paragraph. Non-compliant papers may be stricken.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Settlement and injunctions
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Settlement and injunctions: She usually conducts settlement conferences in jury cases, and may refer a matter to the magistrate judge. Bench-trial cases are automatically referred. For a TRO she schedules a conference as soon as counsel have appeared, requires all counsel to be present unless urgency precludes notice, and rarely grants ex parte TROs. She combines preliminary and permanent injunction hearings when appropriate and usually allows expedited discovery. Proposed findings and conclusions are required in injunction cases.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Pretrial submissions
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Pretrial submissions: About three weeks before trial, the parties submit jointly proposed voir dire, jury instructions, and a verdict sheet, plus motions in limine and trial briefs. Send two copies of points for charge in an editable format. Where you disagree, give each side’s version and rationale. Responses to motions in limine are due within five business days, and no reply is allowed. She usually holds the final pretrial conference about two weeks before trial.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Trial: Court convenes promptly at 9:30 a.m. and may sit until 5:00 or later. She conducts voir dire herself, and counsel submit proposed questions at least five business days before trial. Mark and exchange exhibits before trial and give her two copies in binders with a schedule describing each. No speaking objections, and no continuing objections: state the basis in a word or phrase. Only one lawyer per party may examine a witness. Jurors take notes. She gives counsel her final jury instructions before trial. Counsel must stay within five minutes of the courthouse during deliberations. No food, including bottled water, in the courtroom.

docs.t: Judge Loretta C. Biggs (M.D.N.C.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Loretta C. Biggs, M.D.N.C.. Criminal cases: Follow the term’s scheduling order. Request extensions and continuances well before the term starts under LR 6.1. Submit proposed plea agreements and factual basis documents two business days before the plea hearing if not filed under the schedule, or the case is removed from the calendar. File sentencing memoranda at least two full business days before sentencing. A joint request to change the guideline calculation after the final presentence report must be filed at least three full business days before. File requests for departures and variances at least three business days before sentencing.

docs.t: Judge Catherine C. Eagles (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge Catherine C. Eagles, M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Working copies are not required unless the court requests them, and then they go to the Clerk’s Office within 3 business days. She also refers lawyers to the Standard Preliminary Order for All Civil Cases once it is entered.

docs.t: Judge William L. Osteen Jr. (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge William L. Osteen Jr., M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Working copies are not required unless requested, and then go to the Clerk’s Office within 3 business days. Original papers should be in fixed-pitch Courier New of no smaller than 10 characters per inch, though the court accepts papers formatted under LR 7.1(a). Submit proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law in Word to the court’s case manager.

docs.t: Judge Thomas D. Schroeder (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge Thomas D. Schroeder, M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Working copies are not required unless requested, and then go to the Clerk’s Office within 3 business days.

docs.t: Judge David A. Bragdon (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge David A. Bragdon, M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Submit all pleadings in patent and trademark cases to the Clerk’s Office within 2 business days of filing the original. Other copies, if requested, are due within 2 business days.

docs.t: Judge Lindsey A. Freeman (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge Lindsey A. Freeman, M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Working copies are not required unless requested, and then go to the Clerk’s Office within 3 business days.

docs.t: Judge L. Patrick Auld (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge L. Patrick Auld, M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Working copies are due when the court requests them, or if a brief has more than 10 exhibits. Deliver the brief, with tabs, to the Clerk’s Office within 3 business days of filing on CM/ECF. This applies to non-dispositive motions and Standing Order 30 cases even if the assigned district judge has a different preference.

docs.t: Judge Joi Elizabeth Peake (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge Joi Elizabeth Peake, M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Working copies are not required unless requested, and then go to the Clerk’s Office within 2 business days.

docs.t: Judge JoAnna Gibson McFadden (M.D.N.C.) — Working copies and formatting
docs.x: Judge JoAnna Gibson McFadden, M.D.N.C.. Working copies and formatting: Working copies are not required unless requested, and then go to the Clerk’s Office within 3 business days. She also refers lawyers to the Standard Preliminary Order for All Civil Cases once it is entered.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Chambers
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Chambers: Your point of contact is the courtroom deputy clerk, by email or in writing. Don’t discuss the merits with her or the law clerks, and they won’t say when a ruling will issue.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — AI certification
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. AI certification: Certify at the end of every filing either that no generative AI was used, including in research, or that anything AI influenced was personally reviewed for accuracy and every citation is to a real authority that says what you claim. The certification doesn’t count against page limits, and a filing without it may be stricken without leave to amend.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Diversity jurisdiction
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Diversity jurisdiction: Plead citizenship affirmatively and distinctly. Alleging a party is not a citizen of a state, or only where an individual resides, isn’t enough. For LLCs and other unincorporated entities, name every member and trace citizenship through every layer, and an estate takes the decedent’s citizenship.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Filing basics
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Filing basics: All filings must be text-searchable. A TRO or preliminary injunction request must be made by motion, and a request for expedited consideration must also be emailed to the courtroom deputy. File a proposed order with every motion. Cite the record by docket entry number and CM/ECF page, in the body of the brief and not in footnotes.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Extensions
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Extensions: Extensions, including of discovery deadlines, are granted generally only if you couldn’t reasonably have anticipated the need. Ask promptly, say whether the other side consents, and give a specific timetable. He generally won’t extend page limits, and a request must come at least five days before the deadline.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Discovery disputes: Meet and confer by phone or in person, since letters or email don’t satisfy it unless repeated attempts fail through the adversary’s conduct. If unresolved, file a Joint Statement Regarding Discovery Dispute of three single-spaced pages with the disputed requests attached and a certificate of conferral. He then decides whether to rule on the papers or hold a recorded conference. You need his permission through this process before filing any motion to compel, quash, for a protective order, or for sanctions. All discovery must be initiated so responses are due before the close of discovery, and he won’t enforce side agreements to go past it.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Sealing and experts
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Sealing and experts: He strongly disfavors motions to seal. Protective orders must contain his required sealing language and follow Local Rules Appendix H II(J). Don’t file a motion to exclude expert testimony until after summary judgment unless needed to resolve it.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Motions generally
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Motions generally: Meet and confer before any dispositive motion and certify that you did. Multiple plaintiffs or defendants file one consolidated dispositive motion and one objection to a report and recommendation absent leave. State and develop each argument in the body with particular authority, since he may disregard arguments in footnotes, incorporated by reference, or raised first in a reply.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Failing to respond
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Failing to respond: Under his order, failing to respond timely to any motion is treated as consent and intentional abandonment, and he may grant the motion on that ground alone, even with prejudice. Failing to address part of a motion in a timely response is treated the same way for that part.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Summary judgment
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Summary judgment: He requires strict Local Rule 56.1 practice: a separate statement with one fact per numbered paragraph, a response that must be an admission, a direct refutation with pincites, or one of the listed objections, with the movant’s fact copied before each response, and a separate reply to refuting facts. He may disregard a whole paragraph or filing for one defect and deem facts admitted. A “no evidence” argument isn’t enough for a movant without the burden.

docs.t: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown (N.D. Ga.) — Argument, settlements, exhibits
docs.x: Judge Michael Lawrence Brown, N.D. Ga.. Argument, settlements, exhibits: Oral argument is more likely if a lawyer under five years out of law school will lead it. He won’t approve an FLSA settlement that bars the plaintiff from disclosing the claims or their resolution. Give him and his law clerk each a courtesy copy of any exhibit or demonstrative introduced in court.

docs.t: Judge Emily C. Marks (M.D. Ala.) — Her uniform scheduling order timing
docs.x: Judge Emily C. Marks, M.D. Ala.. Her uniform scheduling order timing: Trial and the pretrial conference are set by the court’s calendar. The proposed pretrial order is due 7 days before the pretrial conference, and dispositive motions are due 120 days before it. The discovery and settlement conference is 30 days before the dispositive motion deadline. Plaintiff’s expert disclosures are due 90 days and defendant’s 60 days before the discovery cutoff. docs.t: Judge Emily C. Marks (M.D. Ala.) — Pretrial and trial dates

docs.x: Judge Nina Morrison, E.D.N.Y.. Excerpts: Written submissions must be text-searchable to the extent practicable (except from pro se litigants). Submit proposed orders and certain documents by email in both PDF and Word to her chambers address, though you needn’t send Word files of stipulations of dismissal or settlement or of extension motions unless asked. Lawyers must enter a notice of appearance on ECF. She encourages less experienced and underrepresented attorneys to take part in court proceedings. If complying with her pre-motion practices would cost you a substantive right or a statutory deadline, you may file the motion on time with an explanation.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Electronic filing standing order (trap)
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Electronic filing standing order (trap): Under the May 6, 2026 standing order, anyone who applies for e-filing privileges must certify understanding of and ability to meet the filing requirements. Court personnel will not e-file for anyone who has been granted e-filing privileges; those unable to e-file may file on paper.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Case management: The judge follows Local Rule 16.1(D) for the initial scheduling conference and does not ask about settlement that early, but schedules mediation unless the parties refuse. The judge assumes the parties want a trial: summary judgment motions are set within 9 months of the conference, the final pretrial conference within 11 months, and trial within 12 months. No status conferences unless a party asks, and no initial pretrial conference in civil cases. Case-management disputes are resolved “baseball arbitrator” style, choosing the more reasonable and proportionate proposal. Bifurcating discovery is possible but usually causes delay. Pro se litigants need not submit a detailed written case-management proposal.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Discovery: The judge typically decides discovery motions personally, on the papers, with no hearing except in extremely rare cases, and adds no requirements beyond Local Rule 37.1(A). Emergency discovery motions are always considered, but calling a motion an emergency does not make it one. General protective orders are encouraged but are not the place to address sealed filings, a practice the judge disfavors. No expert may testify to anything not fully revealed in the expert’s report. Daubert hearings are extremely rare, and Daubert motions should be decided before discovery closes so a substitute expert can be found if needed.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Beyond the Local Rule 7.1(b) page limits there are no added requirements. Reply and sur-reply briefs are welcome, with no page limit, but the judge does not wait for them before ruling. Provide a courtesy copy if exhibits are voluminous. Hearings are typically held on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, usually no more than 10 minutes per side, or 5 for simpler motions. Post-argument briefs are welcome but will not hold up the ruling.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Patent cases
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Patent cases: Patent cases are managed like any other; there is no special patent order. About eight constructions are enough in one case. The judge comes to the Markman hearing with a tentative construction, discusses it, and if either side is dissatisfied hears one expert per side in a one-hour “hot tub.” Jointly agreed written tutorials are welcome.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Pretrial (trap)
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Pretrial (trap): Proposed voir dire, jury instructions and verdict forms, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are due at the latest on the Friday before Monday’s empanelment. Motions in limine are limited to 20 pages and are not typically heard or resolved at the final pretrial conference. Trial briefs are welcome but not required; motions in limine are equally effective. Trial dates are set at the initial case management conference in civil and criminal cases. Exhibits are pre-marked: numbers once in evidence regardless of which party offers them, and letters for identification running A to Z, then AA, AB, AC (not AA, BB, CC). Courtesy copies of trial exhibits are not required but are welcome.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Jury selection: The judge questions the venire, handles excuses, seats the jurors, and has each say a few words about their work. Peremptories go plaintiff or prosecution first, then defense, alternating who goes first each round, with no back-strikes. The judge picks the foreperson. No attorney voir dire. Twelve jurors in civil cases and 2 alternates in criminal cases. Questionnaires are used in high-publicity cases (where a struck system may be preferable) and should be short, preferably one page, focused on knowledge of the case and bias.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Trial: Trial days run 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. In civil cases, openings are generally 15 minutes per side and closings 30, the number of trial days is agreed at the final pretrial conference, and the judge keeps time. No podium requirement and no limit on rounds of examination; rebuttal cases should be rare. Tell the judge beforehand about chalks in openings or closings. At the charge conference the judge explains the proposed charge first and then discusses it. The jury gets a written charge if deliberations go into a second day. Special verdict proposals are considered, though the judge favors general verdicts. In bench trials, do not read depositions aloud; the judge will read them.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: The judge handles criminal discovery personally, usually on the papers, and sets a tentative trial date at the initial conference. Local Rule 117.1(a) governs the initial pretrial conference. Release motions go first to the magistrate judge; hearings are typically held on motions to review a detention order. Sentencing memoranda are welcome but not required, and must arrive in time to read and reflect on. Expedited sentencing is considered when likely incarceration is shorter than the usual preparation time; postponement when it could favor the defendant and the government does not object. Victim impact statements come early, before the guideline calculation, argument, and allocution.

docs.t: Judge William G. Young (D. Mass.) — The Judge’s Common Book
docs.x: Judge William G. Young, D. Mass.. The Judge’s Common Book: The page posts “The Judge’s Common Book,” a collection of judging principles rather than procedures. Its central theme is that trial judges should be on the bench trying cases every day, along with deciding promptly and not being rushed into cutting corners.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. He tries to schedule mediation after fact discovery but doesn’t require it. At the initial conference he sets the whole schedule, including the final pretrial conference and trial, and he rarely holds status conferences.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Discovery: He tells counsel most discovery motions are unnecessary and warns that obstructive lawyers may be sanctioned. He usually refers discovery motions to the magistrate judge, without a hearing. A protective order must say it is subject to Local Rule 7.2. He doesn’t schedule Daubert motions, and most that are filed are denied.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Usually no reply brief without leave of court, granted only for good cause and capped at 10 pages. He requires no courtesy copies of exhibits. He holds hearings on motions to dismiss only sometimes, and on summary judgment only when an issue isn’t sufficiently briefed, usually allowing 15 minutes per side. Post-argument briefs are rare.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Trial: Motions in limine are limited to 10 pages and are usually due two or three weeks before trial, along with requested jury instructions, voir dire questions, and objections to the other side’s witness and exhibit lists. He wants paper copies of those in chambers. Exhibits are marked in one numbered sequence, not as “government” or “defendant” exhibits. He sets time limits for openings, evidence, and closings after consulting counsel. Counsel can’t wander the courtroom, may use a movable podium or none, and sidebars are allowed only when absolutely necessary. In bench trials, proposed findings and conclusions are due before trial.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: He leaves criminal pretrial matters to the magistrate judge, including release motions, and decides suppression motions on the papers unless a hearing is warranted. A sentencing memorandum isn’t required but is strongly advised.

docs.t: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton (D. Mass.) — Remote proceedings
docs.x: Judge Nathaniel M. Gorton, D. Mass.. Remote proceedings: As of Fall 2022 he routinely held no events by Zoom in civil or criminal cases, but would consider it for good cause. His page says there are no COVID-19-related restrictions in his session.

I read the first three and the civil jury trial order here. The other four are posted but I didn’t read them.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Initial scheduling conference
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Initial scheduling conference: His notice treats attendance by the senior lawyers ultimately responsible for the case, and compliance with Local Rule 16.1(B), (C) and (D), as of the utmost importance. A continuance is allowed only if counsel is actually engaged in trial, and noncompliance can bring sanctions under Local Rule 1.3. Initial disclosures under Local Rule 26.2(A) are due within two weeks after the conference, and no formal discovery can start until you comply. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify any party who hasn’t appeared. All future filings must be made electronically unless he grants leave for good cause, and notices and orders go out only by email.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Newer lawyers
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Newer lawyers: His session strongly encourages relatively inexperienced attorneys to take part in all proceedings, including summary judgment arguments and witness examinations. They must be fully prepared and have authority fitting the proceeding, and in an evidentiary hearing of substantial complexity, such as examining a witness at trial, they must be supervised by a more experienced lawyer unless he allows otherwise.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Scheduling order
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Scheduling order: After the conference the order sets deadlines to amend pleadings, designate experts and make their disclosures, finish expert depositions, finish discovery, and file summary judgment motions. Responses to summary judgment are due 14 days later under Local Rule 7.1, and filings must conform to Local Rule 56.1. A further status conference follows, with a joint status report due seven days before. Changes need a motion showing good cause, with affidavits or record references, the reasons, what discovery remains, and a date certain for finishing.

docs.t: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock (D. Mass.) — Civil jury trial
docs.x: Judge Douglas P. Woodlock, D. Mass.. Civil jury trial: Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. until deliberations. A pretrial conference is set about three weeks before trial, attended by trial counsel with settlement authority. A pretrial memorandum is due seven days before that conference, extended only for exceptional cause, and failing to file it can mean dismissal, default or other sanctions. At the same time, file separately your requested jury instructions with authority, any proposed special verdict forms, proposed voir dire questions, and motions in limine. By the first day of trial, before the jury is impaneled, file exhibit lists in his format: undisputed exhibits in one numbered sequence, and contested items in one capital-letter sequence, regardless of which party offers them. During deliberations counsel may leave the courtroom but must be back within 5 minutes of a call from the depu

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Posted orders: Courtesy copies (2006 order): file a paper courtesy copy, stamped “Courtesy Copy: DO NOT SCAN,” of any electronic document relating to a dispositive motion, opposition, reply or sur-reply, with all exhibits. Her order counts motions to dismiss, summary judgment, suppression, preliminary relief, judgment as a matter of law, Daubert motions and motions in limine as dispositive for this purpose. Sealing (2015 order): she generally denies motions to seal whole memoranda and attachments, because filings are presumed open. Redact the public filing and seek to seal only truly confidential material, with a supporting affidavit from a person explaining the need. A party’s agreement or a protective-order designation isn’t enough. If the dispute can’t be resolved, file the full memorandum under seal, then a redacted public version within 7 working days

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial scheduling conference she schedules fact discovery, expert discovery, Daubert briefing, summary judgment briefing, trial and mediation. Counsel should be ready to discuss the facts and legal issues and the amount of discovery needed for settlement. She asks about proportionality and wants to hear if a protective order dispute is likely. Status conferences are rare and only at the lawyers’ request. Don’t assume a continuance will be granted, and last-minute requests short of a true emergency are disfavored.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Discovery: She typically refers discovery motions to the magistrate judge, without a hearing. A protective order doesn’t bind her, and she independently decides what is public in her opinions and filings. Daubert motions are scheduled at the initial conference and shouldn’t be filed as motions in limine just before trial.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: She likes reply and sur-reply briefs, within the 20-page limit under the local rules, but will strike “supplemental” replies. She typically holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, with time limits set as needed. She allows parties to bring new case law to her attention afterward.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Trial: She typically requires a trial brief in civil and criminal cases, sometimes waived if summary judgment briefing was extensive. In civil cases the joint pretrial memorandum and individual trial briefs are due seven days before the final pretrial conference. Deadlines for voir dire, instructions and motions in limine are set at the pretrial conference. Number agreed exhibits and letter contested ones, using her exhibit-list templates. Bring a courtesy copy of trial exhibits in a binder at trial. Counsel must resolve deposition objections before trial and present any that remain so the Court has at least 3 business days to rule. She seats 10 civil jurors, and in bench trials likes proposed findings before trial, supplemented within two weeks after.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: She holds an initial pretrial conference at the close of discovery to complete the pretrial order and set a trial date, always holds a hearing on suppression motions, and resolves release motions herself. A sentencing memorandum is required when the guidelines are disputed or a variance or departure is sought.

docs.t: Judge Patti B. Saris (D. Mass.) — Remote proceedings
docs.x: Judge Patti B. Saris, D. Mass.. Remote proceedings: As of Fall 2022 she typically held Rule 16 conferences, status conferences and non-complex dispositive motion hearings by Zoom, and held criminal trials, pretrials, revocations, sentencings and evidentiary hearings in person. She would consider Zoom for other events on request for good cause.

docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Mediation order
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Mediation order: His page posts one form order, on mediation. Mediation is held by video conference, and lawyers must attend with clients or representatives who have authority to negotiate and commit to settlement terms. Everyone participates in good faith, and all communications stay confidential. Each party gives the court, five days before, a confidential settlement memorandum of no more than five pages: the background and key issues with a breakdown of claimed damages, the strongest and weakest points in each side’s case, and the status of negotiations including each side’s last proposal. Counsel confer first to confirm where settlement proposals stand. The memoranda go by email to the courtroom deputy, are not docketed or shared with the other side, and are returned afterward.
