docs.t: Judge Michael Ponsor (D. Mass.) — Other practices
docs.x: Judge Michael Ponsor, D. Mass.. Other practices: His page posts no other standing orders and no Judicial Forum Survey answers, so check with chambers for scheduling and motion practice.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts one form notice of the initial scheduling conference. It treats attendance by the senior lawyers ultimately responsible for the case, and compliance with Local Rule 16.1(B), (C) and (D) (and 16.6 in patent cases), as of the utmost importance. A continuance is allowed only if counsel is actually engaged in trial, and noncompliance can bring sanctions under Local Rule 1.3. Plaintiff’s counsel must notify any party who hasn’t appeared.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Case management: Normally he sets only the fact discovery schedule at the initial conference and schedules a status conference before fact discovery ends, where he may take up discovery, the schedule, mediation (especially the court-annexed program) and any problems. He generally makes only a general inquiry about settlement. Where e-discovery matters, parties usually negotiate a protocol.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Discovery: He has no typical practice on who decides discovery motions: he refers some to the magistrate judge and decides others himself, and typically holds no hearing. He strictly enforces the time periods in Civil Rule 26, Criminal Rule 16 and Local Rule 116.1 for expert disclosures. A protective order must provide that any later amendment needs the court’s approval. “Emergency” discovery disputes should be rare. With a pro se party he may waive the Local Rule 7.1 consultation requirement.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: He allows reply and sur-reply briefs without a usual page limit, but expects them to be succinct and targeted. For motions with lengthy memoranda or supporting materials he will often ask for courtesy paper copies. He holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment most of the time, with no usual time limits on argument. Post-argument briefs depend on the circumstances, for example a new issue raised at argument.

docs.t: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr. (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge George A. O’Toole Jr., D. Mass.. Criminal matters: Criminal discovery is ordinarily handled by the magistrate judge during pretrial supervision, who also sets the deadline for suppression motions. A release motion goes first to the magistrate judge, and he typically holds a hearing on a motion to review a detention order. A sentencing memorandum isn’t required but is useful, and the government must give advance notice that victim statements will be offered. He answered none of the trial-practice questions in the survey.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Sealing and protective orders (Aug. 6, 2025)
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Sealing and protective orders (Aug. 6, 2025): He generally denies motions to seal whole memoranda and attachments, because filings are presumed open and only compelling reasons justify sealing. Instead, file a redacted public version as an attachment to a motion to file the unredacted document under seal. The motion must follow Local Rule 7.2 and be supported by an affidavit that identifies each redaction by page number and justifies it. It must describe generally what is to be sealed, how long, and the legal grounds. Anyone may oppose within 7 days. If granted, within 7 days file the unredacted version under seal, file the redacted version publicly, and serve the unredacted one on all parties. The parties’ agreement to a confidentiality designation, or a discovery order limiting disclosure, isn’t enough by itself. If you can’t confer or you disagree, co

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Default judgment (Feb. 2, 2026)
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Default judgment (Feb. 2, 2026): A default judgment motion must comply with Rule 55, including affidavits on the damages sought, the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, and that no defaulting party is a minor or incompetent. For a sum certain, also submit a form of order like his Appendix A within 14 days after the motion. For any other amount, submit supporting affidavits within 14 days. The defaulting party may file a substantiated opposition and ask for a hearing within that 14 days, and he takes the motion up on the papers afterward. A noncompliant motion may be denied, with renewal barred for six months and no interest, costs or fees added after the original motion. File the motion within 30 days of the clerk’s order pointing you to this standing order, or file an affidavit showing good cause, or risk dismissal for want of prosecution.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Case management: He usually sends a standard order with a scheduling template that follows Local Rule 16.1. He asks the parties about mediation, and often checks in after fact discovery and before expert expenses. Where ESI is significant, counsel should have a plan, especially if the parties’ ESI capabilities are very unequal. He invites the parties to propose expert deadlines at the outset.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Discovery: He holds a hearing on a discovery dispute if he has open questions after reading the submissions, and often requires or encourages an informal conference under his supervision as part of the Local Rule 37.1 conferral. For bottlenecks, parties can contact his courtroom deputy to arrange a brief phone or Zoom hearing.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Reply briefs are allowed up to 12 pages, due 7 days after the opposition. For a sur-reply, file a motion for leave and attach the proposed submission. He usually holds hearings on motions to dismiss and always on summary judgment, with no fixed time limits, and may ask for supplemental briefing on open questions. No courtesy copies are required.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Mediation: He has a standard pre-mediation order and expects the parties to follow it. He strongly prefers in-person mediation, requires the parties to attend, and discourages trial-style opening statements.

docs.t: Judge Paul G. Levenson (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Paul G. Levenson, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: He will generally postpone or cancel an interim status conference on a joint request, if the parties file a joint status report with a clear update and next steps and represent that all parties agree to exclude time until the next conference. As of Fall 2022, civil status conferences were commonly held by Zoom, and he would consider Zoom for other events when safety or cost warrant.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Protective orders (Sept. 20, 2021)
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Protective orders (Sept. 20, 2021): Any proposed stipulated protective order must include her provision: nothing confidential gets filed until you obtain a ruling on a motion to impound under Local Rule 7.2, and the parties’ confidentiality designations don’t bind the Court. A party sealing its own material must give specific reasons. Before filing another party’s confidential material, confer with the designating party. If you can’t agree, the filing party moves to seal and the designating party must file a supporting statement within two weeks. File redacted versions on the public docket and send unredacted courtesy copies to the Clerk’s Office marked NOT FOR DOCKETING – COURTESY COPY – SEALED FILING. She encourages use of the court’s model protective order, attached to her order, and wants a proposed order filed as soon as practicable.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Summary judgment briefing (Dec. 15, 2021)
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Summary judgment briefing (Dec. 15, 2021): This order applies to consent cases before her. A reply is allowed within 7 days after the opposition, up to 12 double-spaced pages; anything longer, later, or a sur-reply needs leave. For cross-motions the order sets a sequence: plaintiff’s motion (20 pages), defendant’s combined opposition and cross-motion within 30 days (30 pages), plaintiff’s combined reply and opposition within 21 days (20 pages), and defendant’s combined reply and sur-reply within 10 days (15 pages). File one combined statement of undisputed facts, where the opposing party reprints each fact and answers beneath it, and email the deputy clerk a Word copy. File exhibits in chronological order with a descriptive table of contents, and cite exhibits already filed instead of refiling copies. Deliver courtesy copies in a tabbed binder within 2 b

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Courtesy copies (Oct. 7, 2022)
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Courtesy copies (Oct. 7, 2022): Deliver one courtesy copy to the District Court Clerk’s Office within three business days of electronic filing. Her survey answer says she requires courtesy copies of documents over 100 pages.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Other posted orders
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Other posted orders: Her page also posts scheduling orders for referral cases and for consent cases, an initial pretrial order, a standing order encouraging newer lawyers to take courtroom roles, a standing order on protective orders in criminal cases, and a defendant’s waiver of appearance at arraignment. I didn’t read those in full, so check them before you file.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Case management and discovery
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Case management and discovery: After the initial conference she sets at least the end of fact discovery and holds a status conference before fact discovery ends. She asks whether the parties want a mediation referral, and wants to hear about anything unusual in discovery. She holds hearings on discovery motions and wants specifics on relevance and burden, plus a status report if issues are narrowed beforehand. She will hear emergency discovery motions but strongly encourages the parties to work it out or agree to a stay.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: She holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, with no time limits. Replies and sur-replies are allowed up to 12 pages. Post-argument briefs are allowed when she has an open question or the law or facts changed.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Mediation: Her pre-mediation order says: don’t contact the deputy about scheduling, file a motion to continue with several dates, bring counsel and principals with full settlement authority, and submit a confidential memorandum of no more than 5 pages by email 14 days before, marked “Confidential - Not for Docketing.” The memo covers the merits, damages, discovery status and settlement talks. She holds a Zoom conference before the mediation and prefers to mediate in person.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief and sets the trial date and deadlines about three months ahead. She holds an initial pretrial conference on motions in limine, the neutral statement and voir dire. Courtesy copies of exhibits go in a binder several weeks before trial, and uncontested exhibits use one numbered sequence. After the first full day, trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. She seats 8 civil jurors, doesn’t allow attorney voir dire, and lets jurors take notebooks. She dockets a draft jury charge and discusses it with counsel.

docs.t: Judge Jennifer C. Boal (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Jennifer C. Boal, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: She refers a criminal case back to the district judge when discovery is substantially complete. As of Fall 2022 she routinely held status conferences by Zoom, civil and criminal, and considered other Zoom requests case by case.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts a civil scheduling order and a standing order encouraging newer lawyers to take courtroom roles. I didn’t read either in full, so read them before you appear.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial conference he sets fact and expert discovery and doesn’t usually set a trial date then. Be ready to give the estimated number of depositions, whether expert discovery will be needed, and why the discovery period you request is necessary. He asks about the court-sponsored mediation program at every conference and holds a status conference at the close of discovery on discovery, mediation and the trial schedule. He sets a trial date at that status conference.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Discovery: A discovery motion without the Local Rule 7.1 or 37.1 certification is denied without prejudice as a matter of course. He decides after the briefs whether a hearing is needed. He bifurcates discovery when there is a Monell claim. He will hear only true emergencies. Expert designation and deposition dates are in the initial scheduling order, and he doesn’t set a Daubert schedule at the first conference.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: The summary judgment statement of material facts should be a separate document with each fact numbered. Replies and sur-replies are allowed only on motion and only to address specific points in the response, with no page limit. No courtesy copies are required. He holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment only if the motion requires, with no time limits but a request to be mindful of the court’s time. Post-argument briefs are allowed for a previously undiscussed issue raised at the hearing.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Mediation: He requires a confidential mediation statement of no more than four pages, five business days before. It covers the key issues with a breakdown of damages, each side’s strongest and weakest points, the status of negotiations with each side’s last proposal, and the settlement proposal the party thinks is fair. A party with decision-making authority must be present, and any deviation must be requested well in advance. He doesn’t usually invite opening statements and meets with the parties separately.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Trial: Proposed voir dire, instructions, exhibit and witness lists, and motions in limine are typically due one week before the pretrial conference, where he hears and resolves motions in limine. Agreed exhibits are marked by number and contested ones by letter. Trial runs Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and he seats 8 civil jurors.

docs.t: Judge David H. Hennessy (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge David H. Hennessy, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: Be ready at status conferences with an estimate of when the case can go to the district judge, trial or plea needs such as interpreters and digital equipment, and your speedy trial position. He allows phone appearances and cancels a status conference if the parties file a joint memo addressing the local rule and agree to exclude time. He refers the case back when the defendant requests trial or a plea. With a pro se party he is more likely to hold a hearing and issue written orders.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Posted orders: Her page posts a standing order on in-person proceedings during COVID-19 and a Rule 16 scheduling order. I didn’t read either in full, and the COVID order may be out of date, so confirm with chambers.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial conference she sets fact and expert discovery, written and depositions, and the dispositive motion deadlines, and sets a status conference at the close of fact discovery to review discovery, interest in mediation and settlement. She explains the court’s ADR program, and wants any outstanding discovery motions raised at the conference. With a pro se party she holds more frequent interim status conferences.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Discovery: Before a discovery motion, you can call her courtroom clerk to set up a phone conference, and may file letters or joint statements beforehand. She tries to resolve as many issues as she can without motions. If a hearing is set, she orders the parties to confer first to narrow the issues, then hears argument on what’s left. She hears emergency motions when timing is the issue, such as a deposition scheduled for the next day or a looming deadline. She usually asks the parties to agree on and propose their own protective order.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Replies and sur-replies are allowed within a 5 to 8 page limit. She asks for courtesy copies only if filings are voluminous. Whether she holds a hearing on a motion to dismiss or summary judgment depends on the issues, with no time limits on argument. Post-argument submissions are welcome on new issues raised at the hearing.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Mediation: Confidential memos are due about a week before the mediation, with a phone conference five days before to confirm readiness, that an offer and counter-offer have been made, and that the necessary people will attend. The order appears on the docket when mediation is scheduled. She mediates by Zoom or in person, as the parties prefer, and wants the parties present, with exceptions in some cases.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief with a witness list, expected trial length, issues of law, outstanding motions, and a synopsis of the expected evidence. She holds an initial pretrial conference, and deadlines for voir dire, instructions and motions in limine are in the trial scheduling order. She hears and usually resolves motions in limine at the final pretrial conference, and tries to resolve Daubert motions before it. Bring loose-leaf binders of exhibits to the final pretrial conference, and meet beforehand to go over exhibits. She doesn’t allow attorney voir dire. A typical trial day is 9:30 to 1:00 and 2:00 to 3:30.

docs.t: Judge M. Page Kelley (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge M. Page Kelley, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: She refers a criminal case back to the district judge after discovery is complete and the final status conference, or earlier for a Rule 11 hearing or on request. As of Fall 2022 she routinely held civil status conferences and motion hearings by Zoom, left it to a defendant whether to appear by Zoom in a criminal hearing, and allowed Zoom witness testimony in civil cases when the parties agree.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Discovery disputes: call first
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Discovery disputes: call first: Under his standing order you can’t just file a discovery motion. First contact his courtroom deputy, typically by email, with a summary of the issue. He then convenes a telephone conference to try to narrow or resolve it, and only if that fails may you file a discovery motion. If he holds a hearing, he uses it as a working meeting and tries to resolve each issue, often ruling orally from the bench and following with an electronic order. He considers emergency motions when an event is imminent or when one dispute must be resolved before other discovery can go forward. He urges a protective order be filed as early as practicable.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts a sample scheduling and instruction order and a notice of and order on mediation. I didn’t read either in full, so read them before you appear.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Case management: The joint memorandum before the initial conference should include a proposed discovery plan with expert deadlines, which he generally endorses if agreed and reasonable. At the conference he sets all significant discovery phases and the dispositive motion briefing, makes sure the parties know the court’s mediation resources, and asks about ESI volume and any protocol discussions. He holds a status conference before the end of fact discovery. He bifurcates discovery when liability or the correct defendant is genuinely in question.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: He urges parties to keep to the page limits, which he sees exceeded often. Replies and sur-replies need leave but he inclines to grant it if they will help, capped at 7 pages. He asks for courtesy copies only when filings are voluminous. He usually holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, with no hard limits but about 30 minutes per side in mind. Post-argument briefs on specific questions are usually helpful.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Mediation: Each party submits a confidential memorandum of five pages or less, with key exhibits only to help him understand the case. He starts with everyone present, then invites counsel to make short, non-argumentative introductory comments, then holds caucuses. A party with decision-making authority must at least be reachable by phone, and he strongly prefers they attend.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Trial: He requires a trial brief and holds an initial pretrial conference to discuss legal and evidentiary issues, stipulations, witness numbers and trial length. He sets the trial date at a status conference at the end of fact discovery. Voir dire, instructions, exhibit and witness lists, and motions in limine are due around the final pretrial conference, about a week before trial, where he hears and resolves motions in limine and Daubert motions. Courtesy copies of exhibits go in a binder, and exhibits must be pre-marked in a consistent logical way. He sits 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on evidence days and 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. once deliberations begin, and seats 8 or 9 civil jurors. He doesn’t expect to allow attorney voir dire. In bench trials counsel needn’t give a jury-style opening.

docs.t: Judge Donald L. Cabell (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Donald L. Cabell, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: The joint status memorandum is due seven days before a status conference, and when one is late he orders a responsive memorandum by the close of business that day. He refers a case back to the district judge when discovery is complete and dispositive motions are filed or scheduled. As of Fall 2022 he routinely held civil scheduling conferences and most mediations by Zoom, contested motions in person, and most criminal status conferences by Zoom.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Motion practice order (July 24, 2026)
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Motion practice order (July 24, 2026): Follow Local Rules 7.1(a)(2) and 37.1(a) on conferring, and the 20-page limit in Local Rule 7.1(b)(4), which can be exceeded only with leave. A motion to extend a deadline is granted only for good cause and must state the reasons, summarize the discovery that remains, and give a specific date for finishing discovery, joining parties, amending, or moving. File supporting papers separately from the motion, with each attachment as its own attachment whose docket text gives the exhibit number and a short title. Cite the docket as “(Docket No. ___).” A request for oral argument goes in a separate paragraph of the motion or opposition, and without a hearing she decides on the papers.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Discovery motions: confer, then request a conference
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Discovery motions: confer, then request a conference: Before any discovery hearing you must confer, with at least one personal communication such as in person, video or phone, and certify it. Before drafting a motion to compel, for a protective order, to quash, to strike discovery responses, or similar, contact the courtroom deputy and request a brief conference by Zoom. File a joint memorandum of no more than three pages, three days before the conference, outlining the disputed areas and attaching the discovery in dispute. If you still want a motion afterward, file it by the close of fact or expert discovery, whichever applies. She won’t hear disputes from discovery done after the deadline absent good cause. The motion must set out each disputed request and the response, with your position and authority after each.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: An opposition is due 14 days after service, or 21 for summary judgment. The movant may reply as of right within 7 days of the opposition, or 14 for summary judgment, up to 5 pages, and a sur-reply is not permitted. For summary judgment, state facts in a numbered list. The opponent restates each fact in order and responds beneath it, then lists additional facts continuing the numbering, and the reply follows the same format. With cross-motions, defendant files first (20 pages), plaintiff files a combined opposition and cross-motion within 30 days (30 pages), defendant files a combined reply and opposition within 21 days (15 pages), and plaintiff may reply within 14 days (5 pages). She usually holds hearings on summary judgment and decides on a case-by-case basis for motions to dismiss.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Newer lawyers
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Newer lawyers: Normally one lawyer per party argues at a hearing, but she encourages senior lawyers to let lawyers with five or fewer years of experience argue. Tell her before the hearing, and she will allow multiple lawyers to argue for that party.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Case management: Parties must consult and submit an agreed pretrial schedule no later than 7 days before the scheduling conference, addressing the topics in her sample scheduling order. She sets fact and expert discovery, dispositive motion dates, and the next status conference, and holds a status conference near the close of fact discovery. She asks whether the parties want the court’s mediation program, and if there are no dispositive motions or mediation she may set a trial date. She encourages a protective order at the earliest time.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Mediation: Her pre-mediation notice requires counsel and principals with full settlement authority to attend in person. A preliminary settlement conference is held by video, for counsel only. Each party emails a confidential memo of no more than 5 pages, five days before that conference, marked “Confidential - Not for Docketing,” covering the merits, damages with a specific breakdown, discovery status, and settlement talks. To cancel or move the mediation, file a motion with several proposed dates and email the courtroom deputy.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief and holds an initial pretrial conference, setting the trial date after the joint pretrial memorandum estimates the length. She sets deadlines for voir dire, instructions and motions in limine after conferring with counsel. Courtesy copies of exhibits go in a binder and on a flash drive several weeks before trial. Exhibits get unique numbers, with no separate plaintiff or defendant numbering, groups marked with decimals such as 5.1 and 5.2, and numbers don’t change if a document is excluded. Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and she seats 8 civil jurors. She shares a draft charge and verdict form before the charge conference.

docs.t: Judge Jessica D. Hedges (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters and Zoom
docs.x: Judge Jessica D. Hedges, D. Mass.. Criminal matters and Zoom: Joint status memoranda are due seven days before a status conference under the local rules, and she reminds parties to file them on time. She refers a case back to the district judge when discovery is complete. As of Fall 2022 she typically held status conferences by Zoom but always accommodated requests for in-person hearings, and would consider Zoom for non-evidentiary hearings.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts no standing orders. His survey says several practices are still being worked out, and that he will note any special filing format in his pretrial procedural order.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial conference he asks whether the parties have discussed settlement and encourages early mediation. He sets a schedule through discovery to dispositive motions and typically sets a mid-discovery status conference to check on discovery. Expert disclosure deadlines are set then, and a Daubert schedule only at the parties’ request. In cases with large-scale electronic discovery he expects the parties to have a plan on production formats, timelines and search terms. He prefers parties negotiate a confidentiality agreement before seeking a protective order.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Discovery: He typically holds a hearing on discovery motions, and may use it as an informal discussion, but expects the parties to have worked on the issue beforehand. He considers emergency motions when an event is imminent and the dispute couldn’t have been foreseen. He has no added requirements beyond Local Rule 37.1(A).

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Replies and sur-replies need leave, which he typically grants if they will help the court, and they shouldn’t restate earlier arguments. He has no set limit, but a request for leave must say how many pages you want. He usually holds hearings on motions to dismiss, though he may decide a simple legal issue on the papers, and holds them on summary judgment, without time limits. He may request paper courtesy copies for very voluminous filings.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Mediation: Each party submits a confidential memorandum of up to five pages. After introductions, parties move to separate sessions. If you want opening statements first, say so in your memo and briefly explain why. He prefers that a party with decision-making authority attend, though he may allow phone participation.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Trial: He requires a trial brief and holds an initial pretrial conference on legal and evidentiary issues, stipulations, witness numbers and trial length. Voir dire, instructions, witness and exhibit lists, and motions in limine are due before the final pretrial conference, where he hears and resolves motions in limine and Daubert motions. Exhibits must be pre-marked, and you should discuss your marking method with his courtroom deputy. Courtesy copies are due before the final pretrial conference if exhibits are disputed, or at the start of trial. Expect trial days from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. with breaks, and ask for a different schedule in the joint pretrial memorandum. Expect time limits on openings and closings, and say how long you need in that memorandum. He sets the trial date at a status conference after discovery closes.

docs.t: Judge Christopher L. Morgan (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Christopher L. Morgan, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: He refers a criminal case back to the district judge when discovery is complete and adds no requirements beyond Local Rule 116.5.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Posted orders: Her page posts two forms: an order for a pretrial memorandum in jury trials and one for bench trials. I didn’t read them in full, so read them before trial.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Case management: At the initial conference she sets all discovery, dispositive motions, Daubert, and any Markman hearing, subject to change, and asks about mediation and the likelihood of dispositive motions or trial. She holds status conferences every 60 to 90 days to check discovery and whether the schedule can be met. Be ready to name the number and identity of deponents, and to discuss where ESI is and a plan to preserve and retrieve it.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Discovery: She holds a hearing on discovery motions and usually rules orally from the bench. She generally considers emergency motions, and rarely bifurcates discovery, with cost a major factor.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: Replies and sur-replies are allowed within a page limit. She usually holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment, with time limits that vary, and rarely allows post-argument briefs. She asks for courtesy copies only on rare occasions with voluminous documents.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Mediation: Her sample notice orders counsel and parties to attend with full settlement authority, and excuses a party’s presence only by court order. Submit a brief confidential memo on the merits and your settlement position, by fax or email, three business days before, marked “Confidential - Not for docketing” and not served on the other side. If the date conflicts, don’t contact the deputy. Confer and file an assented-to motion to continue with several dates when counsel and principals are available.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief with contested issues of fact and law, proposed jury instructions, contested and stipulated exhibits, and a witness list, with voir dire, instructions and motions in limine due one week before trial. She sets a trial date after discovery and dispositive motions. Courtesy copies of exhibits go in a binder on the first day, and stipulated exhibits are pre-marked, plaintiff by number and defendant by letter. Counsel must use the podium, and she doesn’t allow attorney voir dire. Trial runs 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., and she may limit time that seems excessive.

docs.t: Judge Marianne B. Bowler (D. Mass.) — Criminal matters
docs.x: Judge Marianne B. Bowler, D. Mass.. Criminal matters: She refers a criminal case back to the district judge when the defendant indicates a trial or plea, or there is a dispositive motion schedule.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Posted orders
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Posted orders: His page posts consent procedures for Springfield (2012) and a standing order for attorneys, plus a blank mediation order for Zoom. I didn’t read them in full, so read them before you appear.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Mediation: His mediation order asks each side to send him alone a memorandum of no more than four pages, about five days before, covering the main issues, each side’s strengths and weaknesses, the history of settlement negotiations, and the settlement the party is seeking or would accept. He starts by meeting jointly to put everything on the table and asks each side’s understanding of the last demand or offer. He doesn’t want their bottom or top lines, and then shuttles between the parties. A party with decision-making authority must attend, though he occasionally allows phone participation.

docs.t: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman (D. Mass.) — Other practices
docs.x: Judge Kenneth P. Neiman, D. Mass.. Other practices: He answered none of the survey’s case management, discovery, motion, or trial questions, so check with chambers if you are before him on anything but mediation.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Case management
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Case management: She follows Local Rule 16.1. At the initial conference she usually schedules fact and expert discovery and often waits to schedule dispositive motions until a later status conference, held toward the close of fact discovery. She always asks about mediation, and works with the parties to schedule any discovery needed before settlement talks. Tell her about the substance of the case and likely discovery problems, and she will discuss the best way to present discovery issues, such as motions, letters, or informal conferences.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Discovery
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Discovery: She has no specific requirements beyond Local Rule 37.1(A), but works with counsel on whether full briefing is needed or the issue can be decided in a phone conference. She generally holds substantial hearings on discovery motions, rules from the bench when possible, and usually issues an order, sometimes asking the parties to draft it. She considers real emergencies and rarely rules without letting the other side respond. She schedules Daubert motions closer to trial but prefers to address them early.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Dispositive motions
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Dispositive motions: For summary judgment she wants one document stating the undisputed facts with the opposing party’s response. She generally allows reply briefs, which must be very short and focused, and discourages sur-replies. She holds hearings on motions to dismiss and summary judgment with no time limits, and asks for courtesy copies only on request. Post-argument briefs are possible if she requests them or to bring new cases to her attention.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Mediation
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Mediation: Her electronic order directs counsel to attend with clients or representatives with full settlement authority, and each party to submit a brief confidential memo, marked “Confidential - Not for Docketing,” on the merits and settlement, three business days before. Bring a standard-form settlement agreement if you use one. She has no opening statements, meets each counsel privately beforehand without clients, then meets everyone, then does shuttle diplomacy. A decision-maker must attend, and with permission may occasionally be available by phone.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Trial
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Trial: She requires a trial brief and an initial pretrial conference under the local rules. She sets deadlines with the trial date, usually 1 to 2 weeks before trial, expects motions in limine to be heard at the final pretrial conference, and tries to resolve them as early as possible. Hard copies of exhibits are preferred, with disputed ones filed with the motion. She seats 9 civil jurors, has not allowed attorney voir dire but would consider a request, and reviews the jury charge item by item with counsel. Trial days are 10 to 4 for shorter trials and 9:30 to 1:00 for longer ones.

docs.t: Judge Judith G. Dein (D. Mass.) — Other guidance
docs.x: Judge Judith G. Dein, D. Mass.. Other guidance: She encourages less experienced lawyers to take part in court proceedings, especially discovery hearings. She refers criminal cases back when discovery is complete and usually holds criminal status conferences within a month.

The government files all case-in-chief witness statements in camera, under seal, at least 10 days before trial. Any Jackson v. Denno hearing is held on the day of trial before openings.

Motions to amend must state the effect of the amendment and identify the page, line, and wording of each change, with a Notice of Lodging of the proposed pleading and a redline appendix. Deliver the redline to opposing counsel at least two hours before the L.R. 7-3 conference; if the draft changes, confer again. Default judgment motions are due within 14 days after default against the last defendant or resolution of all other claims, must show subject-matter and personal jurisdiction, and must include any fee and cost request (a later fee motion will be stricken absent good cause). docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Ex parte applications and TROs: Only for extraordinary relief, with a showing of irreparable prejudice and that the movant is without fault or acted with excusable neglect (Mission Power). Decided on the papers; don’t set a hearing. Any opposition or notice of non-opposition is due 24 hours after receipt of the application or 24 hours after it is filed, whichever is earlier. The same deadline applies to TRO oppositions, and the court won’t rule on a TRO until at least 24 hours after service unless notice is excused or justice requires.

docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Continuances and stipulations
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Continuances and stipulations: Good cause only, judged by diligence and prejudice. Requests must be by stipulation, motion, or application with a declaration giving the reasons and any prior continuance requests and their outcome. Stipulations aren’t effective until approved, and every stipulation or request to alter time must propose new dates for all affected deadlines. Criminal cases: confer on new dates and email the courtroom deputy to confirm availability before filing any continuance request. Calendar conflicts: notify both judges’ courtroom deputies at least 3 days ahead and defer to the more senior judge. A “Notice of Unavailability” has no effect and should not be filed.

docs.t: Judge Fred W. Slaughter (C.D. Cal.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Fred W. Slaughter, C.D. Cal.. Sealing: Civil: follow L.R. 79-5. Justify each item under the good cause or compelling reasons standard; blanket claims or meritless requests will be denied. Meet and confer before filing an application to seal, and file a redacted public version where redaction is feasible. Criminal: e-file the application with a proposed order that includes an alternative line in case of denial, then email PDFs and a Word proposed order to FWS_Chambers@cacd.uscourts.gov with the case number and “UNDER SEAL REQUEST” in the subject. Bracket and highlight redacted portions in the unredacted copies. Use a generic cover sheet title if the real title is confidential. Non-paper exhibits go to the Clerk’s intake on USB, not CD.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes: Confer in good faith in person or by phone before seeking relief; consider the expedited joint procedure in LCR 37. Privilege logs must give enough detail to evaluate the claim; for attorney-client privilege, identify the attorney. If immediate involvement is needed, request a telephonic hearing under LCR 7(i); all counsel to the dispute must join the call to chambers at (206) 370-8930.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Default judgment (trap): Support the motion with a declaration and separately state principal, liquidated damages, pre- and post-judgment interest, and attorney’s fees, explaining how each was calculated. Provide evidence of the principal amount (attach the relevant contract portions if contract-based) and of entitlement to liquidated damages. State the interest rate and why, and for prejudgment interest the accrual date and its basis. Fee requests need a basis and a declaration from plaintiff’s counsel on the reasonable amount.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Motion form and length
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Motion form and length: The court may return over-length filings or decline to consider arguments beyond the LCR 7(e) limits. The sheet restates LCR 10 format (double spacing, 12-point text, 10-point footnotes, three inches at the top of page one).

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Sealing
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Sealing: Every motion to seal, including stipulated ones, must describe the documents specifically, give facts justifying sealing, and include a proposed order. Without agreement, file a properly noted motion before or with the document. Give at least 7 days’ notice before filing a document another party claims is confidential so a sealing motion can be filed with it. Tell the court what to do if sealing is denied (e.g., remove rather than unseal). Trial evidence, including confidential material, is generally public.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Mediation and settlement conferences
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Mediation and settlement conferences: In consent cases the judge enters an order stating whether the case is designated for LCR 39.1 mediation; the sample order sets a date to negotiate, has the parties pick and file a mediator (plaintiff applies if they can’t agree), and requires a mediator’s report. A settlement judge generally isn’t appointed until the parties have mediated. The courtroom deputy schedules the conference (Courtroom 12A, Seattle), and the court sets aside the entire day. Each trial attorney attends in person with a client or representative with full authority; failure to bring the right people or participate in good faith may draw costs and fees. Deliver a confidential memo (facts, issues, law, settlement proposal, efforts to date; helpful exhibits allowed) to chambers by 12:00 noon on the set date; don’t file or serve it.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits (trap)
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits (trap): Deliver the original and one copy of exhibits to chambers no later than the pretrial conference date, in three-ring binders with numbered tabs, each exhibit clearly marked. Plaintiff numbers from 1; defendant continues with the next unused number. Don’t list duplicates; once listed in the pretrial order any party may use an exhibit. File exhibit and witness lists and revisions. Misdemeanor trials: unless otherwise directed, give the judge exhibits in tabbed three-ring binders on the trial date. The United States numbers from 1; defendants number from 1A.

docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Jury selection: Civil: tell the court before trial whether the case needs an extra-large pool or individual questioning of each prospective juror, and submit proposed voir dire questions in every case. Criminal: submit proposed voir dire questions five days before trial; only Class A misdemeanor defendants get a jury in misdemeanor cases. Jurors get random numbers, and the lowest-numbered sit in the box. The court describes the case, reads witness lists, has counsel make introductions, and screens for hardship and familiarity; counsel may usually question jurors within time limits the court sets. Challenges for cause are generally heard outside the jury’s presence. docs.t: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida (W.D. Wash.) — Withdrawal and criminal motions
docs.x: Judge Brian A. Tsuchida, W.D. Wash.. Withdrawal and criminal motions: Withdrawal requires leave (GR 2(g)) except for changes within the same firm: file a written motion and supporting affidavit, which may be filed under seal if it contains privileged or prejudicial information. Motions to extend time to indict or file an information must state specific facts meeting the Speedy Trial Act; boilerplate (party agreement, a speedy trial waiver, time to negotiate) is insufficient alone. A defendant seeking the extension normally files a signed waiver. The sample civil consent form is marked “Do Not Electronically File.”

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits: Exhibits are handled electronically: admitted exhibits go to the jury through JEEPS, and DEPS is used for presentation. Before each session, show opposing counsel the exhibits you will offer; unobjected ones are admitted when offered, and objections are raised for ruling before the session opens. Counsel retrieve their own exhibits after trial.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — New lawyers and courtroom rules
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. New lawyers and courtroom rules: The court encourages hearings conducted by lawyers practicing less than seven years, especially those who drafted the briefing; an experienced attorney may supplement their argument or questioning. Leave for supervised Rule 9 interns is freely granted, and multiple attorneys may argue for one party. Turn off mobile devices before entering. Give advance notice to use courtroom video displays. Pronouns and honorifics may be given in signature lines or to the in-court deputy.

Plaintiff makes a demand at least 10 days before, and defendant responds at least one week before, even if the conference is set on shorter notice. docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. Jury selection: The court voir dires a panel equal to the jurors to be seated (8 in most civil cases) plus all peremptory challenges; civil cases have no alternates. Sensitive issues and excuse requests are followed up with individual jurors separately via Zoom, and each panelist excused for cause is replaced before peremptories. Peremptory challenges are exercised simultaneously by written lists; overlapping strikes do not earn extra challenges, and jurors are seated from the lowest-numbered unchallenged panelist.

docs.t: Judge Grady J. Leupold (W.D. Wash.) — ESI and Individualized Trial Program
docs.x: Judge Grady J. Leupold, W.D. Wash.. ESI and Individualized Trial Program: The page posts the district’s Model Agreement Regarding Discovery of ESI (e.g., disclosure of the five most likely custodians within 30 days; the requesting party may add up to 10 search terms within 14 days of the producer’s disclosure). The judge encourages the LCR 39.2 Individualized Trial Program; on agreement the court sets a case management conference, and trial is held within six months of approval.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Filings and contact
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Filings and contact: No courtesy copies unless the court orders otherwise. All PDFs must be text-searchable; PDFs longer than 14 pages need electronic bookmarks, and submissions longer than 14 pages (regardless of word count) need a table of contents. Use slip sheets (“Exhibit A” and nothing more) to separate exhibits. Avoid substantive footnotes; in-line citations preferred. Footnotes must be single spaced and 12-point or larger. Email the courtroom deputy (grant_cogswell@wawd.uscourts.gov) or whiteheadchambers@wawd.uscourts.gov, copying all counsel. No phone calls except emergencies ((206) 370-8700); no faxes. docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Extensions and scheduling (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Extensions and scheduling (trap): Parties may agree to extend the time to answer without filing anything. Initial scheduling order deadlines may be extended by contacting the courtroom deputy, with no stipulation filed. Deadlines falling before the dispositive motions deadline may be extended by a Stipulated Notice (not a motion) in the judge’s prescribed language, only if all parties stipulate (non-opposition won’t do), the deadline was not previously extended, and no hearing or related final-submission date changes. Otherwise dates are firm absent good cause, and the judge generally won’t shorten the gap between the dispositive motion deadline and trial. Don’t file notices of unavailability; they have no effect on deadlines.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Motions (trap): Meet and confer before any Rule 12(b) motion to see if amendment can avoid it; the motion must include a certification of conferral. Don’t oppose a timely motion, or withhold a stipulation, to amend. Daubert motions are due by the dispositive motion deadline and can’t be raised or renewed as motions in limine. Oral argument may be requested but is not granted as a matter of course; the deputy schedules it, and the noting date is not the hearing date. Less experienced attorneys and those from historically underrepresented backgrounds are encouraged to argue, and more than one attorney may argue per party.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Cross-motions for summary judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Cross-motions for summary judgment (trap): Anticipated cross-motions must be briefed in four sequential briefs, not six: opening 8,400 words; combined opening/opposition 10,500; combined opposition/reply 10,500; reply 4,200. The court assumes the defendant files first, but the parties may choose. File a stipulated motion proposing the schedule and word limits before the first brief; all briefing must be complete by the dispositive motion deadline.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Discovery (trap)
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Discovery (trap): Discovery motions are a last resort. Good-faith conferral requires affirmative suggestions and compromise, not just stating positions; the court will deny or strike a motion for failure to confer. Motions must state the grounds and relief with specificity or be denied. The court urges use of the LCR 37(a)(2) expedited joint motion procedure. Don’t file initial disclosures or expert reports unless ordered or at issue. Deposition objections must be concise and non-suggestive (e.g., “Objection, compound”); no conferring with the witness while a question is pending except on privilege; instruct not to answer only to preserve privilege, enforce a court limit, or present a Rule 30(d)(3) motion.

docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Hearings
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Hearings: Hearings are in person in Courtroom 16A, Seattle, unless ordered otherwise. On Zoom (if warranted): each participant needs their own camera and microphone, video on, muted unless speaking, no screenshare, professional attire, a quiet room (not a car); recording is illegal. Telephonic proceedings use the court’s conference line with credentials from the deputy; use a landline if possible and identify yourself each time you speak.

docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Civil juries are 7 to 12 jurors with no alternates. Jury selection is by Zoom in panels of 12–15 unless a party objects and shows good cause. Attorney voir dire typically gets 20 minutes plus 10 minutes of follow-up; each side ordinarily has three peremptories on an alternating strike sheet beginning with plaintiff. Email a Word version of the pretrial order, with witness and exhibit lists, to whiteheadorders@wawd.uscourts.gov when filing it. A sample pretrial conference agenda is posted. docs.t: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead (W.D. Wash.) — Criminal cases
docs.x: Judge Jamal N. Whitehead, W.D. Wash.. Criminal cases: All motions, including motions to continue trial and motions in limine, are due no later than 28 days before trial; motions in limine raised later in a trial brief will be stricken. In multi-defendant cases, consult codefendants about joint or stipulated motions. A motion to continue trial needs a speedy trial waiver running at least 30 days past the proposed new date, and the deputy must first confirm the date fits the calendar. docs.x: Judge James L. Robart, W.D. Wash.. Dispositive motion cutoff: 105-day rule (trap): The dispositive motion cutoff is set 105 days before trial: 30 days for briefing, 45 for the court to decide, and 30 for trial preparation. The judge won’t shorten that gap without an extraordinary basis.

docs.t: Judge James L. Robart (W.D. Wash.) — Default judgment (trap)
docs.x: Judge James L. Robart, W.D. Wash.. Default judgment (trap): Insufficient motions are denied. docs.x: Judge Lauren King, W.D. Wash.. Briefing (trap): No table of authorities and no courtesy copies required. Citations go in the body, not in footnotes (except after explanatory footnotes). docs.x: Judge Lauren King, W.D. Wash.. Cross-motions and motions in limine (trap): Four-brief schedule: plaintiff’s motion (8,400 words, noted 49 days out); defendant’s combined response/cross-motion 21 days later (14,000 words); plaintiff’s combined reply/response 21 days later (8,750 words); defendant’s reply 7 days later (4,200 words). docs.x: Judge Lauren King, W.D. Wash.. Discovery disputes: Confer in good faith before any motion to compel or for protective order; joint submission under LCR 37(a)(2) is encouraged. docs.x: Judge Lauren King, W.D. Wash.. Six to 12 jurors, no alternates, never fewer than seven seated. docs.t: Judge Richard A. Jones (W.D. Wash.) — Motions practice

Oral argument is decided after briefing, and the court will call to schedule it. Overlength motions are disfavored and considered only in extraordinary circumstances set out in detail; file and note them early enough for a ruling before the brief is due, never with the overlength brief. The court may ignore argument beyond LCR 7(e) limits. File stipulations as a “Stipulated Motion”; they may be noted same-day but won’t necessarily be decided then. Deadlines stand until an extension motion is granted, so file well ahead. docs.x: Judge Richard A. Jones, W.D. Wash.. Discovery, sealing, and default judgment: Use the LCR 37 expedited joint procedure where motions are needed. Default judgment motions must comply with LCR 55, be supported by a declaration, and separately state and explain principal, liquidated damages, pre- and post-judgment interest (with accrual date and any non-§ 1961 rate), and fees (with counsel’s declaration). Attach the relevant contract portions; amounts whose calculation is unclear won’t be awarded.

docs.t: Judge Theresa L. Fricke (W.D. Wash.) — Conduct at trial (trap)
docs.x: Judge Theresa L. Fricke, W.D. Wash.. Conduct at trial (trap): Stand when court opens or recesses, when the jury enters or exits, and when addressing or addressed by the court; examine witnesses from the lectern; ask permission before approaching the bench. Address remarks to the court and refer to everyone by surname. One attorney per side per witness; the lawyer objecting on direct is the one who cross-examines. State only the legal ground for an objection, with no argument unless asked. Sidebar conferences are presumptively not tolerated except in extraordinary, unforeseen circumstances; hold issues for the next recess. Make stipulation offers privately, and don’t express personal opinions in opening or argument. The posted rules also carry COVID-era protocols (examining from counsel table, distancing, face coverings, sidebars held with the jury out of the room).

docs.t: Judge Theresa L. Fricke (W.D. Wash.) — Trial exhibits
docs.x: Judge Theresa L. Fricke, W.D. Wash.. Trial exhibits: All exhibits are handled electronically; admitted exhibits go to the jury through JEEPS, and DEPS is used for presentation. Display any offered exhibit to opposing counsel electronically first; hand any needed hard copy to the courtroom deputy. Before each trial session, show opposing counsel the exhibits you will offer; unobjected exhibits are admitted when offered, and objections are presented for ruling before the session opens. Counsel are responsible for retrieving their exhibits after trial.

docs.t: Judge Theresa L. Fricke (W.D. Wash.) — Jury selection
docs.x: Judge Theresa L. Fricke, W.D. Wash.. Jury selection: The court voir dires a panel equal to the jurors to be seated (8 in most civil cases) plus all peremptory challenges; there are no alternates in civil cases (e.g., 14 panelists for 8 jurors with 3 peremptories per side). Sensitive follow-up is done individually via Zoom. Jurors excused for cause are replaced before peremptories. Peremptories are exercised simultaneously by written list; overlapping strikes earn no extra challenges, and the jury is seated from the lowest-numbered unchallenged panelists.

docs.t: Judge Theresa L. Fricke (W.D. Wash.) — Remote proceedings
docs.x: Judge Theresa L. Fricke, W.D. Wash.. Remote proceedings: The posted example remote jury selection order (July 16, 2021) used ZoomGov with a 25-juror pool, one 15-minute round of questioning per party, and court-asked questions submitted in advance. Counsel emailed each participant’s name, email, phone, and role to the courtroom deputy. Recording, screenshots, or retransmission are prohibited; participants not actively involved stay muted with video off; raise a hand to object; proceedings stop if a necessary participant disconnects. Dress as for court and use your full name as the screen name. The page also posts a reprinted 2020 bar article with general remote-advocacy tips (master the technology, camera and lighting, mute discipline, low-tech backup).

docs.t: Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers (N.D. Cal.) — Summary judgment (major traps)
docs.x: Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, N.D. Cal.. Summary judgment (major traps): No summary judgment motion without leave: first file a letter (three single-spaced pages max, at least seven business days before your proposed date) requesting an in-person pre-filing conference; opponents respond in three pages within three business days. Not required if a party is pro se, or in habeas or Social Security cases. One motion per side, 25 pages. Cross-motions go inside the opposition (25 pages, 14 days after the motion); reply 15 pages, 7 days later. Separate statements are required in her table format (issue, fact, pincited evidence, response); 15 pages, response 5 more. Lead counsel must sign an attestation that the cited evidence fairly supports or disputes the facts. Highlight relied-on lines; file only highlighted deposition excerpts, never full transcripts. Evidentiary objections go in the brief

docs.x: Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, N.D. Cal.. Discovery: No discovery motions without leave. docs.t: Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers (N.D. Cal.) — Calendar and contact
docs.x: Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, N.D. Cal.. Calendar and contact: No schedule change without a signed order and good cause (diligence and prejudice). Ask for deadline extensions well before the deadline; requests leaving her less than two weeks between the last brief and the hearing are likely denied. docs.t: Judge Phyllis J. Hamilton (N.D. Cal.) — Removed cases (trap)
docs.x: Judge Phyllis J. Hamilton, N.D. Cal.. Removed cases (trap): Within 10 days of removal, the removing defendant must file and serve a statement saying: whether all served defendants joined; whether removal came more than 30 days after the first defendant was served; for diversity removals, whether any served defendant is a California citizen, and the citizenship of every named party (including every member or partner of non-corporate parties). Plaintiff may respond within 10 days. Non-jurisdictional remand motions within 30 days of removal (28 U.S.C. § 1447(c)).

docs.t: Judge Phyllis J. Hamilton (N.D. Cal.) — Discovery disputes
docs.x: Judge Phyllis J. Hamilton, N.D. Cal.. Discovery disputes: If email, letter, or phone conferring fails, the parties must confer face to face by videoconference; refusing risks sanctions. Within 10 business days after that, file a Joint Letter (five pages max) describing every disputed issue with each side’s final position and proposed resolution. Applies to subpoenaed non-parties too.

docs.t: Judge Phyllis J. Hamilton (N.D. Cal.) — Protective orders and trial
docs.x: Judge Phyllis J. Hamilton, N.D. Cal.. Protective orders and trial: No broad carte-blanche sealing provisions; any sealing provision must follow Civil L.R. 79-5. File a redline against the district’s model protective or ESI order and email a Word version to pjhpo@cand.uscourts.gov. Documents offered as trial exhibits lose confidentiality absent the most compelling reasons; request protection in writing by the date pretrial papers are due.

docs.t: Judge Jon S. Tigar (N.D. Cal.) — Motions and briefs (traps)
docs.x: Judge Jon S. Tigar, N.D. Cal.. Motions and briefs (traps): Civil motions Thursdays at 2 p.m., by Zoom unless ordered otherwise (pretrial conferences and trials in person). Filing deadlines are 5 p.m. Page limits for ordinary motions: 15 pages opening and opposition, 10 reply (the local-rule limits apply only to summary judgment, class certification, PI, class settlement, and claim construction). Page enlargements rarely granted. One summary judgment motion per party (affiliates count as one). Cross-motions: four briefs only (25, 25, 20, 15 pages), with a stipulated schedule first; the last brief at least 21 days before the hearing. Extension or continuance requests at least three business days ahead; opposition to an administrative motion by noon one business day before the deadline. Footnotes sparing, 12-point minimum; Westlaw cites for unpublished cases; text-searchable PDFs.

docs.t: Judge Jon S. Tigar (N.D. Cal.) — Discovery

docs.t: Judge Jon S. Tigar (N.D. Cal.) — Copies, settlement, and service
docs.x: Judge Jon S. Tigar, N.D. Cal.. Plaintiff must serve this order and the CMC standing order within five days of filing or reassignment.

docs.t: Judge Vince Chhabria (N.D. Cal.) — Sealing (major trap)
docs.x: Judge Vince Chhabria, N.D. Cal.. Sealing (major trap): He almost always denies sealing motions and sanctions frivolous or overbroad ones. State the standard (compelling reasons or good cause), justify each document specifically, highlight redactions; vague “competitive harm” isn’t enough. Overbroad requests risk everything going public.

docs.t: Judge Vince Chhabria (N.D. Cal.) — Hearings, emergencies, and discovery
docs.x: Judge Vince Chhabria, N.D. Cal.. docs.x: Judge Vince Chhabria, N.D. Cal.. docs.t: Judge Beth Labson Freeman (N.D. Cal.) — Trial

docs.x: Judge Beth Labson Freeman, N.D. Cal.. Criminal trials: Joint pretrial statement (per Crim. docs.t: Judge Maria E. Garcia (D. Conn.) — Rule 26(f) reports and status reports
docs.x: Judge Maria E. Garcia, D. Conn.. Rule 26(f) reports and status reports: File a carefully considered, timely 26(f) report; the judge usually defers to agreed schedules unless the case is mismanaged but urges realistic deadlines, and resolves scheduling disputes by telephone conference. A court-ordered Joint Status Report must state (a) the particular status of discovery, pending motions, and anything threatening Scheduling Order compliance; (b) interest in a settlement referral to a magistrate judge; and (c) estimated trial length.

docs.t: Judge Maria E. Garcia (D. Conn.) — Criminal detention and bond motions (trap)
docs.x: Judge Maria E. Garcia, D. Conn.. Criminal detention and bond motions (trap): In a CR case before a district judge, Judge Garcia may not get notice of all filings. Email a copy of any detention, bond, or release-conditions motion the judge may handle to the courtroom deputy, and for emergency or time-sensitive relief also call chambers at 203-773-2022.

docs.t: Judge Maria E. Garcia (D. Conn.) — Joint trial memorandum (trap)
docs.x: Judge Maria E. Garcia, D. Conn.. Joint trial memorandum (trap): The judge’s instructions modify the District’s Standing Order Regarding Trial Memoranda in Civil Cases. The memorandum must be truly joint, not combined separate memoranda, and two paper copies with all attachments go to the court at submission. Before preparing it, exchange witness, exhibit, and deposition lists. Witness entries include a summary, expected duration, and whether the witness is likely or only if needed; expert entries add the area of expertise, the expert’s report, and a CV. Objections to witnesses or exhibits must state grounds and authority, with a brief counterstatement from the proponent. Exhibits are tagged starting at Plaintiff’s 1 and Defendant’s 501, with multiple parties coordinating to avoid duplicate numbers. docs.t: Judge Maria E. Garcia (D. Conn.) — Motions in limine and jury materials
docs.x: Judge Maria E. Garcia, D. Conn.. Motions in limine and jury materials: File motions in limine, each as a separate ECF document with a memorandum, the same day as the Joint Trial Memorandum; objections are due within 7 days unless otherwise ordered. For jury trials only, attach a jointly agreed brief description of the case to read to the panel, proposed voir dire (supplemental questions on the docket no later than 24 hours before jury selection), case-specific jury instructions with authority (no general instructions), and proposed verdict forms. State whether courtroom technology is needed and submit the Request for Courtroom Technology Form at least 2 weeks before trial, or use may be precluded.

docs.t: Judge Robert A. Richardson (D. Conn.) — Oral argument
docs.x: Judge Robert A. Richardson, D. Conn.. Oral argument: Argument is at the judge’s discretion, with no set argument days; the judge tries to accommodate counsel’s schedules. A party that feels strongly should request argument in a letter accompanying the motion. To give junior lawyers courtroom experience, the court is open to more than one lawyer arguing for a party where a junior lawyer familiar with the matter will argue. The judge occasionally rules from the bench, especially on discovery or urgent matters.
